name: XMem

paper.title: XMem: Long-Term Video Object Segmentation with an Atkinson-Shiffrin Memory Model

construction.unit: one feature element per pixel at stride 16: a 64-d key with a shrinkage scalar and a 512-d value per object
construction.kept_as: learned features of past frames and their predicted masks (no pixels kept)
construction.processing: every 5th frame the query key is copied as a memory key and a value encoder turns image + predicted mask into the value; the GRU state is updated every frame
construction.writer: trained networks: ResNet-50 query encoder, ResNet-18 value encoder, GRU

organization.structure: three tiers after Atkinson-Shiffrin: sensory (GRU state), working (recent memory frames), long-term (compact prototypes)
organization.stores: sensory h (64 channels); working memory: first frame + latest frames, 5 to 10 frames; long-term memory: up to 10,000 prototype elements
organization.index: memory keys compared with query keys by an anisotropic L2 similarity (shrinkage per memory key, selection per query channel)

management.operations: when working memory reaches 10 frames, the 5 oldest frames other than the first become candidates: the 128 most-used elements are kept as prototypes and their values are rebuilt as a similarity-weighted average of all candidate values (potentiation)
management.forgetting: least-frequently-used eviction of long-term prototypes once 10,000 elements are reached; usage = accumulated top-k attention / time in memory

retrieval.query: the current frame's key at every pixel, with its selection weights
retrieval.candidates: all working and long-term memory keys
retrieval.selection: top 30 by similarity per query pixel, softmax, weighted sum of the values
retrieval.budget: top-k 30 per query pixel; the memory holds T·HW + L elements (T ≤ 10 frames, L ≤ 10,000)

use.context: readout feature F (512 channels per pixel) together with the sensory state h and the encoder's skip features
use.reasoning: one decoder pass per frame gives the mask; objects are merged by soft aggregation

classify.note: Reading is attention over every stored key; the similarity is learned, and the top-30 cut per query pixel is a fixed rule.

stages.ingestion: Given the first frame and its object mask, XMem processes the video frame by frame and predicts a mask for each new frame.
stages.construction: Every 5th frame the frame's key (copied from the query encoder) and a value (image + predicted mask through the value encoder) are added to working memory; the GRU sensory state is refreshed every frame, with a deep update from the value encoder on memory frames.
stages.organization: Three stores: a sensory GRU state, a working memory of the first frame plus recent memory frames (5-10), and a long-term memory of compact prototypes (up to 10,000 elements).
stages.update: When working memory reaches 10 frames, the 5 oldest non-first frames are consolidated: the 128 most-used elements become prototypes whose values average all candidate values by key similarity; least-used prototypes are evicted when long-term memory is full.
stages.retrieval: Each pixel of the query frame compares its key with every working and long-term key by anisotropic L2 similarity, keeps the top 30, and reads a softmax-weighted sum of their values.
stages.answer: The decoder combines the readout, the sensory state and skip features into a mask per object.
stages.learning: All networks are trained end to end on static-image pretraining, then YouTubeVOS and DAVIS (optionally BL30K), with 8-frame sequences so the sensory memory learns.

summary: Video object segmentation with three feature memories (sensory, working, long-term); working-memory frames are consolidated into a small set of usage-selected prototypes so GPU memory stays bounded on very long videos.
notes: VENUE: ECCV 2022 main (listed on the ECVA open-access page, paper 568, ECCV_2022 papers; arXiv comment 'Accepted to ECCV 2022'). PDF read from arXiv 2207.07115v2. CODE: hkchengrex/XMem at f3b841d (Nov 2024; the inference and memory files are unchanged since 2023 apart from GUI and compatibility fixes). Not an LLM memory: keys/values are CNN features, 'answer' is the segmentation mask. Result rows use answer_model 'none (end-to-end VOS network)' so rows of one table stay comparable. DESIGN: §3.1-3.6, §4, App. D; code inference/memory_manager.py, kv_memory_store.py, model/memory_util.py.

sources.paper: arXiv 2207.07115v2 (PDF read 2026-09-30); ECCV 2022 version on ecva.net
sources.code_note: Latest commit (15 Nov 2024, docs only). The inference core and memory manager have had no algorithmic change since the July 2022 release; later commits touch the GUI, MPS support and numpy compatibility. The paper's footnote points to this repository.

abstract.text: XMem segments a target object through long videos with three feature memories modelled on the Atkinson-Shiffrin theory: a sensory memory updated every frame, a high-resolution working memory of recent frames, and a compact long-term memory. When working memory fills up, its most-used elements are consolidated into long-term prototypes, which keeps GPU memory bounded without compressing new features right away. A new similarity function with per-key confidence and per-channel selection governs how the query reads memory. XMem clearly beats earlier methods on long videos while matching the best methods on standard short-video benchmarks.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: New frames enter working memory at full resolution; only when it holds 10 frames are the 5 oldest (never the first) squeezed into 128 prototypes, a 6328% compression.
Which elements survive is decided by usage: how much attention each element received while in working memory.
Reading is plain attention with a top-30 cut per pixel over working and long-term memory together; the sensory GRU state goes straight to the decoder.

units.name: Working-memory element
units.role: one pixel (stride 16) of a memory frame
units.made_by: query encoder (key) and value encoder (value), every 5th frame

fields.name: key
fields.what: 64-d feature of the frame, copied from the query encoder

fields.name: shrinkage s
fields.what: per-key confidence ≥ 1 that sharpens or widens the key's influence

fields.name: selection e
fields.what: per-channel weights of the frame; used only when the element is chosen as a prototype, to weight the potentiation similarity

fields.name: value
fields.what: 512-d feature per object from the image and the predicted mask

fields.name: usage
fields.what: accumulated top-k attention divided by the number of reads since insertion; ranks elements for consolidation (and, in long-term memory, eviction)

units.name: Long-term prototype
units.role: a consolidated element kept for the rest of the video unless evicted

fields.name: key
fields.what: key of a high-usage candidate element, kept as is

fields.name: value
fields.what: softmax-weighted average of all candidate values by key similarity to the prototype

fields.name: shrinkage
fields.what: averaged the same way as the value

units.name: Sensory memory
units.role: short-term state that tracks position and motion
units.made_by: GRU on decoder features every frame; a second GRU on value-encoder features on memory frames (deep update)

fields.name: h
fields.what: 64-channel hidden state per object at stride 16, zero at the start

write.how: GRU refreshes h from multi-scale decoder features every frame; on memory frames a separate GRU uses value-encoder features instead (deep update)
every r-th frame (and any frame with a given mask) the key and a new value are appended to working memory
when working memory holds 10 frames, the first frame and the latest 4 stay; the 5 frames in between are candidates and the 128 elements with the highest usage become prototype keys
write.out: compression 6328% from working to long-term memory

write.how: each prototype's value becomes a softmax average of all candidate values, weighted by key similarity to the prototype (no top-k here); candidates are then deleted from working memory
before adding prototypes, if long-term memory is within 128 of its limit, the least-used prototypes are removed
write.out: about 3,900 frames' worth of information at r = 10 (App. D)
write.src: paper §3.3, App. D; code memory_manager.py L186-L187, kv_memory_store.py L135-L156

read.how: ResNet-50 features at stride 16; 3×3 convolutions give the key q and the selection e (sigmoid)

read.scores: query key vs every working and long-term key
read.how: anisotropic L2: negative squared distance weighted per channel by e and scaled per key by s
read.src: paper §3.2, Eq. 2, App. I; code memory_util.py L7-L39

read.how: for each query pixel keep the 30 highest similarities, softmax them, zero the rest; the attention mass is added to each element's usage
read.src: paper §4; code memory_util.py L41-L65, memory_manager.py L70-L119

read.how: weighted sum of the selected values gives F (512 channels per pixel)
decoder fuses F with the sensory state h and the query encoder's skip features, upsamples to stride 4 and outputs a logit per object; objects are merged by soft aggregation

answer_context.sees: readout F from working + long-term memory, sensory state h, and the query frame's own features
answer_context.format: feature maps concatenated in the decoder; no text
excludes: memory elements outside each pixel's top 30
includes: first-frame features (always kept in working memory)

compression.what: long-term prototypes vs working-memory candidates per consolidation
compression.basis: §4 states a 6328% compression ratio for T min 5, T max 10, P 128 (Table 6: 12625% at P 64, 3164% at P 256).

compression.what: maximum GPU memory, Long-time Video 3× (LT max 10,000)
compression.basis: 1,515 MB for XMem (App. D, Table S1); the paper does not give a no-consolidation baseline in the same units, so no ratio.

numbers.label: GPU memory cap
numbers.value: never above 1.4 GB with LT max 10,000

numbers.label: Frames before memory runs out without eviction (6 GB)
Speed
numbers.value: 22.6 FPS on DAVIS 2017 and YouTubeVOS 2018; 29.6 on DAVIS 2016 (V100)

numbers.label: Training
numbers.value: about 35 hours on two RTX A6000

paper_vs_code.code: similarity is also divided by √64 before the softmax

paper_vs_code.paper: long-term usage (for eviction) is always tracked
paper_vs_code.code: tracked only when the video is long enough to fill long-term memory (frames / 5 × 128 ≥ 10,000); shorter videos never evict anyway

paper_vs_code.topic: Memory insertion rate on Long-time Video
paper_vs_code.code: eval.py defaults to 5; the r = 10 run is a command-line flag given in docs/INFERENCE.md

open_questions: Without long-term memory the model scores slightly higher on the short sets (85.9 vs 85.7 on YouTubeVOS 2018, Table 4), so consolidation buys bounded memory and speed, not accuracy, on short videos.
Long-time Video has only three videos; the 3× variant plays them back and forth, so it tests memory size rather than new content.
Usage-based and random prototype selection differ by 0.3 J&F at P = 128 (Table 6), within the reported spread; potentiation (87.9 → 90.0) matters more than the selection rule.

key_numbers.value: 5 to 10 frames, first frame always kept

components.model: ResNet-50 without the last stage + 3×3 conv heads

ablation.src: paper Tables 4-8 (Long-time rows are means of 5 insertion offsets)

discussion.takeaway: Keeping several memories at different time scales, and consolidating working memory into a few heavily used prototypes only when it fills, lets video segmentation run on long videos with bounded GPU memory and no loss on short ones.

claims.claim: A single feature memory ties accuracy to memory cost; separate stores break that link.
claims.evidence: Fig. 1: methods with growing memory must insert sparsely and drop on long videos. §1

claims.claim: Clearly better than prior work on long videos.
claims.evidence: Long-time Video 3×: 90.0 J&F vs 84.6 STCN and 83.8 AFB-URR; 1×→3× change +0.2. Table 1

claims.claim: On par with the best short-video methods, and faster.
claims.evidence: YouTubeVOS 2018 85.7 vs AOT 85.5; DAVIS 2017 val 86.2 vs STCN 85.4; 22.6 FPS on DAVIS 2017 vs 20.2 STCN and 18.0 AOT. Table 2
Long-time 3×: 90.0 vs 87.3 eager compression, 87.3 sparse insertion, 85.5 local window. Table 7

claims.claim: Both similarity scaling terms help together.
claims.evidence: 86.2 with both vs 85.1 with neither on DAVIS 2017. Table 5

limits: Fails on very fast objects or heavy motion blur, where even the per-frame sensory memory cannot keep up (§4.4, App. C).
A stronger sensory memory with a larger receptive field might help (§4.4).
reading: Removing long-term memory slightly raises short-video scores (85.9 G, 86.3 J&F); the long-term store pays off only on long videos, where the ablation cannot run it without memory limits (n/a).

Table 1 baselines were re-run with reduced memory insertion to fit in memory, with 5 offsets; baseline numbers on the short sets (Table 2-3) are not said to be re-run except AOT on YouTubeVOS and the re-timed FPS.
r differs by dataset (10 on Long-time Video, 5 on the short sets; 3 in the multi-scale runs of App. H).
The selection term is stored with working-memory elements but only used to potentiate prototypes; long-term prototypes keep no selection term.
Default long-term size (10,000) is far above what Long-time Video needs: 1,000 elements already give 89.5 vs 90.0 (Table S1).
